chapters.title: Who Is the Elect Lady?
chapters.teaser: John addresses a mysterious woman and her children — quite possibly a church in disguise.
body: The letter opens "unto the elect lady and her children" (v.1), and closes with greetings from "the children of thy elect sister" (v.13). It reads like a personal note to a real woman and her family — but many readers, ancient and modern, have suspected the "lady" is a literary figure for a local congregation, with her "children" as its members and her "sister" a sister church.

The ambiguity may be deliberate. A letter like this, warning about dangerous traveling teachers (v.10-11), would circulate among house churches; language that works as both personal courtesy and coded address for a congregation lets the same short note do double duty, whether the elder had one household or a whole church in mind.

chapters.title: Truth and Love, Inseparable
chapters.teaser: The letter's opening piles up the word "truth" before ever mentioning love — then binds the two together.
body: In just the first two verses, "truth" appears four times: John loves the lady "in the truth," as do "all they that have known the truth," for the sake of "the truth's sake, which dwelleth in us." Only after that foundation is laid does he move to "grace, mercy, and peace... in truth and love" (v.3).

The sequence matters. For John, love isn't a free-floating sentiment that can attach to anything; it's love in truth, love that has content and boundaries. Verse 6 makes the fusion explicit: "this is love, that we walk after his commandments." Love and doctrine aren't rivals here — love is what walking in the truth looks like in practice.

chapters.title: Not a New Commandment
chapters.teaser: John reminds his readers that loving one another was never a new idea — just an old one worth repeating.
body: "Now I beseech thee, lady, not as though I wrote a new commandment unto thee, but that which we had from the beginning, that we love one another" (v.5). The wording is nearly identical to 1 John 2:7-8 — this short letter is clearly written by the same hand, applying the same core teaching to a specific, local situation.

There's something almost weary and tender in the repetition — as if John knows he's said this before and will say it again, because a command this basic never stops needing to be restated. Continuity with what "ye have heard from the beginning" (v.6) is treated as a virtue, not a lack of imagination.

chapters.title: Don't Even Say Hello
chapters.teaser: John gives startlingly harsh advice: refuse hospitality to teachers who deny Christ's incarnation.
body: "If there come any unto you, and bring not this doctrine, receive him not into your house, neither bid him God speed" (v.10) sounds inhospitable by any normal standard — but it addresses a specific ancient problem. Itinerant teachers depended on being welcomed into homes; hosting one was effectively funding and endorsing their message and its spread to others.

The doctrine at stake is named plainly in verse 7: deceivers "confess not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh." This is the same denial 1 John targets — a Christ without real flesh, without a real death. John's logic in verse 11 is blunt: "he that biddeth him God speed is partaker of his evil deeds." Hospitality, in this case, isn't neutral kindness; it's material support for a message John considers corrosive to the gospel itself.

chapters.title: Preferring Presence Over Paper
chapters.teaser: The letter closes wishing it didn't have to be a letter at all.
body: "Having many things to write unto you, I would not write with paper and ink: but I trust to come unto you, and speak face to face, that our joy may be full" (v.12) is a small, human moment inside a letter otherwise focused on doctrine and discipline. Even necessary written correction, John implies, is a poor substitute for real presence.

It's a fitting close to one of the Bible's shortest books: for all its warnings about false teachers, the letter's deepest instinct is relational, not merely regulatory. The goal isn't just correct belief maintained at a distance — it's restored, face-to-face fellowship, joy made "full" the way 1 John 1:4 had already promised.
